Casablanca sideboard

A sideboard from the first Memphis collection, covered entirely in sponge-patterned laminate.

Source
V&A: Casablanca sideboard (W.14:1 to 6-1990)
Creator
Ettore Sottsass (Junior); manufactured by Memphis
Made
1981
Style
Memphis (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Loud, anthropomorphic, irreverent, postmodern
Evidence
Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from the V&A IIIF server to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.
Reviewed
25 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A says the sideboard was part of the first Memphis furniture collection, made of plastic laminate over fibreboard. Sottsass designed it for storage and display and as a room divider; the angled arms are meant to hold wine bottles. V&A record.

The V&A links the laminate to American diner interiors and 1950s kitchen furniture, and notes that the furniture was too expensive for the average customer despite its “low taste” sources. V&A record.

The physical description names a sponged pattern in red, black, white, and yellow. V&A record.

Observed

  • A central column carries a tall gray-and-white mottled door panel, a yellow-and-black mottled drawer, and a solid black lower section.
  • Red shelves with black speckles branch from the column: angled arms at the top, long diagonal arms at the sides, and V-shaped cradles lower down.
  • Every visible surface except the black base carries a mottled, sponge-like print.
  • The outline is symmetrical and reads as a figure with raised arms.

Why it belongs

Where the Carlton uses many flat colors, the Casablanca uses three patterned laminates. Both show that Memphis pattern is applied to whole surfaces, not used as trim.

Borrow

Cover whole panels in one coarse mottled texture and change the color from panel to panel.

Use a symmetrical, figure-like outline with diagonal arms to make a practical object look like a character.
